machine: Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 / Radeon 8060S / XDNA2, 128 GB, Arch (Omarchy), Linux 7.2.15; power profile performance. Two kinds of figures. Until 21:45 another session's LLM server (a 35B model) kept the GPU at 95-100% busy, so the GPU and DRAM (which the NPU kernel is bound by) were shared: every section but one below is from then, comparing runs taken in turn under that load. The section with_the_gpu_to_itself is the exception: a turn with nobody else on the GPU, whose controls match the morning's quiet-machine figures.
software: llama.cpp b10944 Linux Vulkan release, Mesa 26.2.5 RADV, xrt 2.21.75; zest before: e54ff8c (whole_array_bfp_rtp kernel, restructured loop); zest after: the by-column kernel with feed-forward chains and resident activations (8fa7414), then the row split (the commit this record comes with)

with_the_gpu_to_itself.when: 21:50-22:12, a turn on the GPU held through the machine's scheduler: nobody else on the GPU (the other session's LLM server had ended), other sessions' CPU work at a load average of 3-8. GPU alone and the build before reproduce the morning's quiet figures (365 / 346 and 303 / 300 against 367 / 349 and 301 / 298), so these stand as quiet-machine numbers.

row_split_every_piece_shared.when: 2026-11-19, 02:22-02:35, a turn on the GPU and the NPU held through the machine's scheduler, nobody else on the GPU, load average 2-8 from other sessions' CPU work. GPU alone and zest without the split reproduce the evening's figures (343.6 and 322.5 at 2,048 tokens against 346.0 and 323.8).
row_split_every_piece_shared.what_changed: In the 27B's linear-attention layers (39 of the 52 on the NPU) the piece with the qkv multiply and the piece with the feed-forward block each end with a view that computes nothing: a transpose of the piece's own result (qkv_mixed_transposed) for an op outside it, or a reshape of the next layer's recurrent state (cache_r_l<n> (reshaped)). llama.cpp's scheduler leaves a view where it falls in the node order, so these sit in the piece before them, and the row view refused the whole piece for a tensor whose rows don't run along its last dimension: 76 of 218 pieces a prompt, 2.6 s of the 3.5 s spent in pieces. (The evening's guess, an op done in place, was wrong: with that allowed, a rerun at 00:50 gave the same 353.0 and the same 142 shared pieces.) A view is now part of the GPU's share only if an op of the piece reads it; all 218 pieces are shared.

findings: The by-column kernel is at least as fast as the one before on every shape timed (1-4% faster under this load), with the same answers bit for bit.

A memtile DMA channel that is waiting for its lock has already loaded its next buffer descriptor: a length written to the descriptor then applies only from the one after. Resetting the channel and starting it again at its first descriptor makes it reload.

Chains remove a tenth of the host passes and a quarter to a third of the pass workers' time, but prefill moved only from 190.8 to 196.2 tokens/s (kernel change included): inside the pieces the NPU's own time is now what the host waits on.
With the GPU to itself: 300.0 tokens/s at 2,048 tokens before, 305.6 with the by-column kernel and chains, 323.8 with resident activations as well (+8%), against 346.0 for the GPU alone.

The row split (GGML_XDNA_SPLIT, off by default) passes its tests and moves the answers toward the GPU's. With every piece shared (2026-11-19) a 50% split gives 431.5 tokens/s at 2,048 tokens against 343.6 for the GPU alone and 322.5 for zest without it, and 469.1 with all 64 layers on the NPU. The evening before, sharing two thirds of the pieces, it gave 353.8 (359.4): views that only follow a piece's last op had kept the largest pieces whole. With a second job generating tokens on the GPU throughout it still leads: 290.7 against 237.0 for the GPU alone and 199.7 for zest without it (the evening's 229 against 196-260, where it seemed to lose, was the build that left the largest pieces whole, in different windows).

Keeping each column's row block of A in its memtile for the call (K up to 5,440) makes those calls 15-18% faster on a quiet machine (26.5-27 TFLOPS) and takes DRAM out of their way: a resident gate/up call moves 427 MB instead of 822. What holds them then is each core's own 32-bit streams (B's 9,216-byte tile per K chunk).
